strengths: Addresses a practically important and underexplored issue: dataset quality, duplication, and train/test leakage in a widely-used remote sensing benchmark (CrowdAI Mapping Challenge Dataset), which if valid, has significant implications for the building footprint extraction literature.

The perceptual hashing pipeline (DCT-based hashing plus augmentation-aware hash comparison) is simple, computationally cheap, and easily reproducible/generalizable to other datasets without requiring pretrained feature extractors.
Provides a reasonably comprehensive survey of prior work that uses the CrowdAI dataset, situating the contribution's relevance to a broad swath of the community (Table 1).

Includes both quantitative (Table 2) and qualitative (Figures 1-2) evidence supporting the duplication/leakage claims, including examples of models reproducing erroneous ground-truth annotations on leaked validation images.
Releases (or claims to release) code and a deduplicated dataset variant, which could be a useful community resource if properly delivered.
weaknesses: The core methodological contribution is minimal novelty: perceptual (DCT-based) hashing for near-duplicate detection is a decades-old, standard technique, and the paper does not propose any new algorithmic advance beyond applying it plus simple augmentation-based hash matching; this limits the technical/methodological contribution expected at CVPR.

No validation of the deduplication pipeline's accuracy (e.g., false positive/negative rates of hash collisions, sensitivity to hash length/threshold choices, comparison against alternative methods such as the self-supervised copy-detection descriptors mentioned in related work) is provided, so the reliability of the reported leakage percentages is not rigorously established.

The paper's central 'overfitting' claim (Section 4, Figure 2) is only supported by a handful of qualitative examples for two methods (PolyWorld, HiSup) and no quantitative re-evaluation of any method on the deduplicated split; this is a serious evidentiary gap given that the paper claims to 'potentially invalidate' ~11 papers listed in Table 1.

No experiments are conducted on the newly proposed deduplicated dataset to show how model performance changes (e.g., retraining/re-evaluating a baseline model on the cleaned split vs. the official split) — without this, the practical impact/usefulness of the contribution is not demonstrated empirically.

The paper does not report basic parameters/hyperparameters of the hashing scheme (hash size, downsampling factor d, similarity/collision threshold, whether exact bit match or Hamming-distance threshold is used) in enough detail for full reproducibility.
Placeholder/incomplete text ('publicly available at' with no URL, in both abstract and contributions) suggests the manuscript was not fully finalized prior to submission.

The scope is narrow (a single dataset and application domain), and the described technique is not really presented or evaluated as a generalizable tool beyond this one case study, despite the title's broader framing ('Large Scale Image Datasets').

Discussion of why/how the CrowdAI dataset came to have such severe duplication (e.g., overlapping tiling from SpaceNet source imagery) is largely absent, which would strengthen the analysis and help contextualize whether 'near-duplicate' via hashing might sometimes reflect legitimately overlapping-but-distinct scenes rather than true copies.

No statistical/error analysis of hash collisions (e.g., could perceptually similar but distinct scenes, such as parking lots or repetitive suburban tracts, cause false-positive duplicate detection using an 8x8 DCT hash) undermines confidence in the precise leakage percentages reported to two decimal places.

strengths: Addresses a legitimately important and under-examined issue: benchmark dataset quality (duplication and train/val leakage) in a widely-used remote sensing dataset (CrowdAI Mapping Challenge), which if true has real implications for the validity of a substantial body of prior building-footprint extraction literature.

The proposed pipeline (perceptual hashing plus explicit handling of rotation/flip augmented duplicates) is simple, computationally cheap, and easy to reproduce/apply to other datasets without requiring pretrained feature extractors.
Provides concrete quantitative summaries (Table 2) and illustrative qualitative examples (Figure 1) of leaked/duplicated image pairs that make the claims easy to visually verify.
The intended contribution -- releasing a cleaned/de-duplicated version of the dataset and open-sourcing the pipeline -- would be useful to the community if properly validated.
weaknesses: The central 'overfitting' claim, which is used to argue that prior state-of-the-art results are 'potentially invalidated,' is never actually tested: no method is retrained or re-evaluated on the de-duplicated splits, and no quantitative performance comparison (leaked vs. non-leaked test performance) is provided. The claim rests entirely on two qualitative figure examples (Fig. 2), which is insufficient evidence for such a strong assertion.

The technical contribution is minimal: the pipeline is a straightforward application of a standard perceptual hashing (DCT-based pHash) algorithm with rotation/flip augmentation checks; no novel algorithmic component, no comparison against alternative hashing schemes (dHash, wavelet hash) or the self-supervised copy-detection methods discussed in related work, and no ablation on hash size/threshold choices.

Critical methodological details are missing: Algorithm 1 does not specify how 'collisions' are actually determined (exact hash equality vs. a Hamming-distance threshold), nor any analysis of the pHash's false-positive/false-negative rate. Without manual verification of a sample of detected 'duplicates,' the reliability of the headline percentages (90%, 93%) cannot be fully trusted.

Numbers are inconsistent and confusingly reported between the abstract and the body: the abstract states 'nearly 250k (~90%) training images were identical,' but this figure is not directly derived or explained in the results/methodology; the body only explicitly reports 95,241 (33.9%) exact train/val duplicates and 107,913 (38.4%) after augmentation, leaving the reader to infer the 90% figure indirectly from the final unique-image counts.

Only rotation and flip augmentations are considered for 'augmented duplicate' detection; other common augmentations (scaling, cropping, color jitter, slight resampling) that could also cause leakage are not investigated, understating or mischaracterizing the true scope of duplication/leakage.

There is a reference/citation inconsistency: Figure 2 attributes predictions to 'PolyWorld [12],' but reference [12] in the bibliography is actually a duplicate entry of Li et al.'s 'Topological Map Extraction from Overhead Images' (same as [11]), not Zorzi et al.'s PolyWorld (which is correctly listed as [24] elsewhere). This kind of bibliographic error undermines confidence in the paper's overall care and rigor.

The paper is thin in technical depth and reads more like a dataset technical report/erratum than a full CVPR-caliber paper; there is no new model, no new benchmark protocol validation, and no experiments demonstrating that the proposed de-duplicated split actually yields more reliable/generalizable evaluation (e.g., by training a baseline model on it and showing meaningful differences from the leaked-split results).
The related work section is largely an enumerative list of papers that use the CrowdAI dataset without deeper synthesis or comparison to other dataset-auditing works beyond a short paragraph.

The choice of which duplicate image to retain is stated to be 'arbitrary,' with no attempt to prefer higher-quality annotations, which is a missed opportunity given the paper's own claims about annotation quality issues.

strengths: Addresses a real and impactful problem: the CrowdAI Mapping Challenge dataset is heavily used in the building-footprint extraction literature (the paper lists 11+ CVPR/ICCV/ISPRS papers relying on it), so uncovering severe duplication and train/val leakage has significant downstream value for the community.

The pipeline (perceptual hashing + DCT-based hash collision detection, extended to rotation/flip-augmented duplicates) is simple, computationally cheap, and easy to reproduce/adopt without requiring pretrained feature extractors, which is a reasonable practical advantage over embedding-based dedup methods.
The quantitative findings are striking and clearly presented (Table 2): ~90% train duplication, ~93% val-in-train leakage, and a systematic breakdown across official/augmented/unique splits.

Qualitative examples (Fig. 1, Fig. 2) provide intuitive, convincing illustrations of both the leakage phenomenon and its downstream effect (models reproducing incorrect/incomplete ground-truth annotations), lending face-validity to the overfitting claim.
The paper commits to releasing the deduplicated dataset and code, which would be a useful community resource regardless of the paper's own technical depth.
weaknesses: No quantitative re-evaluation of any SOTA method (e.g., PolyWorld, HiSup) on the deduplicated/leakage-free split. The 'overfitting' claim rests solely on a handful of qualitative examples (Fig. 2) rather than measured performance drops (IoU, AP, boundary metrics) before/after deduplication, which is the most important evidence needed to support the paper's central claim.

The technical contribution is minimal: the method is a direct, off-the-shelf application of a standard perceptual (DCT pHash) algorithm plus simple rotation/flip augmentation matching; no new algorithmic insight, hashing scheme, or theoretical analysis is proposed.

No analysis of the reliability of the pHash-based matching itself: no reported false-positive/false-negative rate, no ablation on hash size/threshold/downsampling factor d, and no human-verification study confirming that hash collisions genuinely correspond to (near-)identical images rather than visually similar-but-distinct scenes.

The final deduplicated dataset is drastically smaller (~29.5k total unique images vs. 341k original), yet the paper does not discuss or assess how much this reduction alone affects trainability/generalization, nor validate that the new 90/10 split itself avoids near-duplicate leakage beyond exact/augmented hash matches (e.g., near-duplicate crops or overlapping patches from the same footprint could still leak).

Generalizability claims ('drop-in pipeline...for large-scale image datasets') are not empirically supported beyond the single CrowdAI case study; no experiments on another dataset are shown despite this being advertised as a general contribution.

Presentation issues: the abstract/paper repeatedly omit the actual code/dataset URL ('publicly available at' with no link), several numeric inconsistencies appear between abstract (~250k duplicates, 56k leaked) and Results section (95,241 exact duplicates, 56,368 leaked, 250k not fully reconciled with the ~90% duplication figure), which could confuse readers about the exact pipeline stage each number corresponds to.

The related-work discussion of alternative dedup approaches (self-supervised descriptors, LSH) is largely descriptive; no empirical comparison against these alternatives is provided to justify why pHash is preferable in this setting (e.g., in terms of dedup precision/recall) beyond an appeal to computational simplicity.

Contribution is primarily an empirical dataset audit rather than a novel method or benchmark; while valuable as a community service, its scientific/methodological depth for a CVPR paper is limited absent stronger quantitative validation of the overfitting hypothesis.

strengths: Addresses a genuinely important and underexplored problem: the AICrowd Mapping Challenge dataset, widely used in building footprint extraction literature, is shown to have severe duplication (~89-97%) and train/val/test leakage, which is a valuable and actionable finding for the community.

The quantitative evidence is thorough and well-organized: multiple tables report overlap percentages across official and augmented splits for three datasets, with consistent methodology applied across all of them.

The supplementary analysis linking leakage to overfitting is a strong and convincing addition -- splitting the AICrowd test set into 'seen' vs 'unseen' images and showing a HiSup pretrained model performs substantially worse on unseen images (AP 65.4 vs 79.7) provides direct causal evidence that reported benchmark numbers are inflated by leakage, going beyond simple correlation.

Qualitative examples (Figs 2-6) convincingly illustrate near-identical/rotated duplicate image pairs across splits, and Figure 3 shows two SOTA methods (PolyWorld, HiSup) reproducing erroneous ground-truth annotations, supporting the overfitting claim.

The comparison between perceptual hashing and average hashing (main text Table 4 and supplementary benchmark with synthetic ground-truth duplicates, Table 6) adds a degree of methodological validation and shows pHash has a favorable precision/recall trade-off versus aHash.

The paper is transparent about limitations (sensitivity to augmentation choice, lack of invariance to more complex geometric transforms) and about false positives in INRIA/SpaceNet (Figs 7-8), which adds credibility rather than overstating findings.

The pipeline itself (DCT-based perceptual hashing) is simple, computationally cheap (4ms/image), and easily reproducible/applicable to other large-scale datasets, which is a practical contribution even though the underlying hashing technique is not novel.
weaknesses: The core technical contribution (perceptual/DCT-based hashing for near-duplicate detection) is not novel -- pHash is a well-established, decades-old technique, and the paper's main claim to originality rests almost entirely on the empirical audit of the AICrowd dataset rather than any new method; this limits the paper's contribution to computer vision/pattern recognition methodology.

The method is restricted to detecting exact duplicates and a fixed set of augmentations (90/180/270 rotations, h/v flips); it explicitly cannot detect near-duplicates from crops, scale changes, color jitter, or other common augmentations, which likely means reported leakage/duplication numbers are a lower bound and the method's generality is overstated relative to its narrow scope.

The choice of Hamming distance threshold = 0 for 'collision' is not justified or ablated; a threshold-based analysis (varying Hamming distance) would strengthen claims about sensitivity/specificity of the approach, especially since bit depth of 64 is asserted as 'sufficient' without quantitative justification.

The false-positive analysis for INRIA and SpaceNet (waterbodies, no-data rasters) is only qualitative/anecdotal (a handful of visual examples) rather than a systematic characterization of how many of the reported 'overlaps' in Tables 1-2 are true vs. false positives, which weakens the claim that these datasets are 'clean.'

The de-duplication procedure retains an 'arbitrarily' selected image from each duplicate cluster, which could itself introduce distributional bias (e.g., systematically favoring certain image content) that is not discussed or analyzed.

The dramatic reduction of the AICrowd training set from 280,741 to 15,392 images (~94% reduction) raises questions about whether the remaining set is representative/sufficiently large for retraining models to verify the claimed overfitting hypothesis directly (i.e., no retrained model on the cleaned dataset is shown, only inference-time seen/unseen splitting on an existing checkpoint).

Related work section on de-duplication techniques (CE-Dedup, LSH, QHash, self-supervised descriptors) is discussed but not empirically compared against on the AICrowd dataset, so claims that perceptual hashing is preferable to these alternatives are not substantiated experimentally.

The paper reports and critiques other published works' benchmark scores (PolyWorld, HiSup, etc.) as being invalidated by leakage, but does not show how these methods' actual reported metrics change after retraining/re-evaluating on a properly de-duplicated split, aside from the single HiSup seen/unseen inference experiment; broader validation across the ~10 cited affected methods would substantially strengthen the impact claim.

Some presentation issues: the paper reports both 89% (abstract) and multiple other overlapping percentages (93%, 97%, 33.92%) across different subsections without a single clear, consistent headline statistic, which can be confusing to readers trying to gauge the overall severity of the issue.

This work is fundamentally a dataset-audit/analysis paper rather than a new algorithmic or modeling contribution, which, while valuable to the community, may have limited fit and novelty relative to typical CVPR technical contributions focused on new models, architectures, or theoretical insights.

strengths: Identifies a practically important and previously under-reported issue: severe duplication and train/val/test leakage in the widely-used AICrowd Mapping Challenge building-footprint dataset, which is used by numerous published methods (PolyWorld, HiSup, etc.).

Provides a reasonably thorough quantitative audit (Tables 1-4) across three datasets and multiple split combinations, plus qualitative examples (Figs. 2-6) that make the leakage instances easy to verify visually.

Cross-validates the perceptual-hashing pipeline against average hashing and against a constructed synthetic benchmark with known ground-truth duplicates (Table 6, supplementary), giving some confidence that the detected duplicates are not simply hashing artifacts.

Connects the data-quality issue to a concrete downstream consequence by splitting the AICrowd test set into 'seen' vs 'unseen' images and showing a pretrained HiSup checkpoint performs markedly worse on unseen images (supplementary Table 5), supporting the overfitting/inflated-benchmark claim with a quantitative (not just anecdotal) result.
The proposed pipeline is simple, fast (ms-level per image), and easy for other researchers to adopt for quick dataset sanity checks.
weaknesses: Limited technical/methodological novelty: the core technique is off-the-shelf perceptual hashing (pHash/DCT) with augmentation-based invariance to rotations/flips; no new algorithm, learning component, or dataset-specific innovation is introduced beyond applying a known tool to a new corpus.

Headline statistics are inconsistent across the paper: the abstract cites ~90% training duplication and 93% validation leakage, the contribution bullets cite 89% duplication and 97% leakage, and Section 3.2 separately reports 38.72% duplication — these appear to refer to different specific measurements but are not clearly reconciled, which is confusing and undermines confidence in the reported numbers.

The method is inherently restricted to exact/augmented (rotation/flip) duplicates and cannot detect near-duplicates, resized/cropped overlaps, or sliding-window tile overlaps common in remote-sensing datasets (adjacent/overlapping geographic tiles) — a significant blind spot for the very domain being studied, acknowledged only briefly as a limitation.

The 'overfitting' demonstration is based on a single model/checkpoint (HiSup) and only two qualitative failure examples in the main text; broader validation across several of the many cited SOTA methods trained on AICrowd would substantially strengthen the causal claim linking leakage to inflated benchmark numbers.

No experiment retrains or re-benchmarks any model on the proposed de-duplicated/leakage-free splits to show how reported rankings or absolute performance actually change — the paper stops at identifying and removing contamination without demonstrating the corrected downstream impact.
Claims of general applicability to other large-scale datasets (ImageNet, COCO, Cityscapes, LAION) in the conclusion are speculative and not empirically demonstrated anywhere in the paper.

Design choices such as the 64-bit hash depth and zero Hamming-distance threshold are not ablated; no sensitivity analysis is given for how these choices affect detection recall/precision beyond the single synthetic benchmark.

As primarily a dataset-audit/empirical-finding paper without a new model, representation, or algorithm, the contribution may be better suited to a datasets-and-benchmarks track than a core CVPR methods track, limiting its fit and technical contribution for this venue.

strengths: Identifies and rigorously documents a severe, previously unrecognized data quality problem (extensive duplication and train/val/test leakage) in the AICrowd Mapping Challenge dataset, a benchmark widely used by numerous state-of-the-art building footprint extraction papers; this is a genuine service to the community.

The perceptual hashing pipeline is simple, fast (4ms/image), easy to reproduce, and dataset-agnostic, making it practically adoptable by other researchers auditing large-scale geospatial or other image datasets.

The claims are corroborated by multiple lines of evidence: (1) quantitative overlap tables across official and augmented splits for three datasets, (2) a controlled synthetic benchmark with known ground-truth duplicates (Table 6) showing pHash achieves near-perfect precision/recall versus average hashing, (3) qualitative examples of leaked/duplicate image pairs, and (4) a seen-vs-unseen test split analysis (supplementary Table 5) and qualitative examples (Fig. 3) showing that a SOTA model (HiSup) reproduces erroneous training annotations and performs markedly worse on unseen images — directly linking the dataset flaw to inflated benchmark numbers.

Good negative controls: applying the same pipeline to INRIA and SpaceNet, which are shown to be largely clean (with false positives explained as low-information rasters/no-data tiles), strengthens confidence that the AICrowd findings are not an artifact of the method itself.
Clear, well-organized presentation with informative figures/tables, and an explicit, honest limitations section.
weaknesses: The technical contribution is modest: the core method is standard perceptual hashing (DCT-based pHash) combined with augmentation-based matching, both well-established techniques; the paper's novelty lies almost entirely in the empirical audit rather than in a new algorithmic contribution, which is a limiting factor for a venue like CVPR that typically expects methodological advances.

The detection scope is restricted to exact/augmented duplicates (0 Hamming distance, 90/180/270 rotations and flips); it does not address near-duplicates, partial overlaps between adjacent satellite tiles, crops, or scale/brightness changes, which are plausible in satellite tiling pipelines and could mean the leakage percentages reported are a lower bound rather than a complete picture.

No experiments retraining or re-evaluating building-footprint models on the actual de-duplicated/leakage-free AICrowd splits are shown; the paper stops at flagging the problem and shows only a post-hoc seen/unseen split analysis on an existing pretrained checkpoint, rather than demonstrating what "corrected" benchmark numbers would look like after retraining on the cleaned ~15k-image training set.

The final cleaned training set is drastically smaller (15,392 of 280,741 images, ~5.5%), raising concern about whether the corrected dataset remains practically useful for training; this important consequence is not discussed or analyzed in the paper.

Minor inconsistencies between the abstract/intro summary numbers (e.g., ~90%/93% duplication and leakage) and the more precise numbers in the results section (89.55%/97.04%, etc.) could confuse readers and should be reconciled.

The scope of the study is narrow (three building-footprint datasets), and while the authors claim general applicability to other large-scale datasets (ImageNet, COCO, Cityscapes, LAION), no experiments are provided to substantiate this generalization claim.
